lines: Casey Morgan
+1 (555) 010-7731 | casey.morgan@example.com | example.com/portfolio/cmorgan
EDUCATION
Lakeshore University | B.A. in Cognitive Science | Metro City, USA | Sep 2015 - May 2019
EXPERIENCE
Harborview Surf School | Surf Instructor | Metro City, USA | Aug 2025 - Present
- Taught weekend group lessons to beginners aged 8 to 60, keeping each class to one instructor for every six students.
- Ran the rental desk's morning equipment checks and logged board and wetsuit repairs for the shop owner.
Northwind Health | UX Research Associate | Metro City, USA | Jul 2019 - Feb 2022
- Raised the patient app's Net Promoter Score from 6.1 to 8.4, calculated as the average 0-10 recommendation rating across 2,000 monthly survey responses.
- Interviewed 40 patients about appointment reminders; the findings led to a two-way text reminder that cut missed appointments from 14% to 9%.
- Writes the screener and consent templates for all patient studies, cutting study setup time from two weeks to three days.
- Tested the telehealth waiting-room screens with 16 older patients; the revised layout cut support calls about joining a video visit by 30%.
Pinegrove Financial | Senior UX Researcher | Metro City, USA | Mar 2022 - Jun 2025
- Led research on the mobile onboarding flow, testing three prototypes with 24 new customers; the shipped design raised completed sign-ups from 41% to 58% in the quarter after launch.
- Improved dispute-form completion by 40% by splitting the form into three short steps with saved progress.
- Ran 18 moderated usability sessions a quarter from a recruiting panel of 400 customers, so every major release was tested with real account holders before launch.

- Synthesizing 60 interviews, 400 survey responses and 18 months of support tickets through affinity mapping, journey mapping and a tagged clip library, cut repeat support calls about statements by 23%.
- Raised the onboarding flow's System Usability Scale score from 68 to 104 across two rounds of moderated testing with 20 customers.
- Trained 12 product managers to run their own unmoderated tests with a shared script template, which doubled the number of tests run each quarter.
PROJECTS
Accessible Transit Map | Independent Project | Figma | Sep 2024 - Present
- Redesigned a city transit map for screen-reader and low-vision riders, and tested it with 12 participants on timed route-finding tasks.
- Measured the redesign with timed tasks: median route-finding time fell from 95 to 62 seconds and errors from 11 to 3 across the 12 sessions.
- Raised task success by 20% across 12 participants, from 65% to 85%, with audio landmarks and high-contrast line colors.
Community Clinic Booking Redesign | Volunteer, Team of 3 | Figma | Mar 2023 - Aug 2023
- Conducted user interviews and created wireframes for a free clinic's online booking flow.
- Ten clinic patients were recruited and two rounds of hallway testing were run, and the six issues that stopped first-time users were fixed.
- Wrote the clinic's volunteer handbook for maintaining the booking pages, which two later volunteer teams used to add Spanish-language booking.
SKILLS
Tools: Figma, screen-reader testing (VoiceOver, NVDA)
Methods: moderated and unmoderated usability testing, interviews, surveys, A/B testing

items.says: The experience entries are not in newest-first order.
items.because: Northwind appears above the newer Pinegrove role, which may confuse a reader scanning the chronology.

items.says: Harborview takes two bullets and appears before the UX roles despite being unrelated to the UX research story.
items.because: Its prominent placement and space can distract from the more relevant UX experience.

items.says: Education appears before Experience and Projects.
items.because: The work history now carries more weight than the degree, so readers reach the strongest evidence later.

items.says: The teaching and equipment-check duties give the unrelated Harborview role too much space.
items.because: Neither duty connects to the UX research experience that anchors the résumé.

items.says: The line labels an average recommendation rating as Net Promoter Score.
items.because: NPS is the percentage of promoters minus detractors, not the average rating.

items.says: The line gives the outcome but not the work that produced it.
items.because: A reader cannot tell what UX research or product change contributed to the result.

items.says: The rating-calculation explanation is lengthy.
The strongest line in the Northwind entry does not appear first.
items.because: Opening with its link between interviews, a change, and fewer missed appointments would bring the clearer outcome to readers sooner.

items.says: “Writes” incorrectly presents work in a role that ended in February 2022 as ongoing.
items.because: The present-tense claim conflicts with the role’s end date.

items.says: The 30% reduction in support calls has no stated baseline or comparison period.
The 40% dispute-form completion claim lacks before-and-after rates and a comparison.
items.because: A reader cannot judge the size of the improvement or tell whether 40% means a relative increase or percentage points.

items.says: The repeated “by” makes the sentence awkward.
The explanation after the usability sessions is longer than needed.
The statement-support result is buried after a long list of sources and methods.
items.because: A scanning reader reaches the 23% reduction only after several research inputs and methods.

items.says: The 23% reduction in repeat support calls has no stated baseline or comparison period.
“Synthesizing” is inconsistent with completed work and leaves the sentence without a clear main verb.
items.because: Its present-participle form makes the action harder to follow.

items.says: A System Usability Scale score of 104 is outside the valid range.
items.because: Standard SUS scores range from 0 to 100.

items.says: “Which doubled” can refer to the shared script template rather than the training.
The first project bullet gives the test setup but no observed outcome.
items.because: The participant count shows the test’s scale, not whether the redesign helped riders.

items.says: The first project bullet repeats the participant count and task setup in the next bullet.
The results bullet describes the evaluation but not how the map was redesigned.
items.because: It does not show the design skill or approach behind the results.

items.says: The results bullet repeats the timed-task setup and participant count from the previous bullet.
The change from 65% to 85% is 20 percentage points, not 20%.
items.because: The relative increase from 65% is about 30.8%.

items.says: The line names the work but not its effect.
items.because: A reader cannot tell whether the redesign improved booking or otherwise helped the clinic.

items.says: “Online” adds little to the description of a digital booking flow.
The line gives the number of issues fixed but no post-fix evidence.
items.because: A reader cannot tell whether the fixes made booking easier or helped more first-time users complete it.

items.says: The six issues fixed appear after the recruitment and testing details.
The passive phrasing hides your role in recruiting, testing, and fixing the issues.
“Which two later volunteer teams used” has an unclear antecedent.
